\chapter{Esto, Eso, Aquello --- Pointing at What Has No Name}
\label{ch:esto-eso-aquello}
\hlchaptermodality{224}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something I cannot name, or at a whole situation.}

I can point at something I cannot name, or at a whole situation.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[esto · eso · aquello]{esto · eso · aquello — pointing at what has no name yet}

\label{lesson:ES-C59-esto-eso-aquello}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Este libro}, \emph{esa casa}. Both pointing words agreed with a noun.

But what do you say when there \textbf{is} no noun — when you do not know what the thing is, or when the thing is not a thing at all?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third set}]
There is one more form of each, ending in \textbf{-o}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{esto}} & this, here, whatever it is \\
\emph{\textbf{eso}} & that, by you, whatever it is \\
\emph{\textbf{aquello}} & that, over there, whatever it is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

These never sit in front of a noun. They \textbf{are} the noun.

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Qué es} \emph{\textbf{esto}}\emph{?} — What is this?
\end{quote}

\emph{Este} could not ask that: it needs a word to lean on, and the whole point of the question is that you have not got one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine — you learned that in chapter one, and it has held ever since. So what gender is \emph{esto}?

\textbf{Neither.} It is the one leftover of a third gender Latin had and Spanish otherwise abandoned, kept for exactly this job: pointing at what has not been sorted into a gender, \textbf{because it has not been named}.

Which is also how you point at a whole situation — \emph{Eso está bien.} Not a book, not a house; the thing just said. Nothing there has a gender, so the form that agrees with nothing fits.

Name it, and agreement returns: \emph{¿Qué es esto?} — \emph{Es un libro.} — \emph{Ah, ese libro.}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿Qué es esto?}
  \item \emph{esto}, \emph{eso}, \emph{aquello}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When do you use the \emph{-o} form? (When there is \textbf{no noun} — you cannot name it, or it is a whole situation.)

And can \emph{esto} stand in front of a noun? (\textbf{No.} It \emph{is} the noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
